451.event_title: President Harding and the Ohio Gang
451.event: After his election in 1920, Warren G. Harding gave high office to a circle of political friends and allies, many from his home state, who became known as the Ohio Gang, among them Attorney General Harry Daugherty, Interior Secretary Albert B. Fall and Veterans Bureau head Charles R. Forbes. Investigations after Harding's death in 1923 exposed widespread corruption: Forbes was imprisoned for fraud and bribery at the Veterans Bureau, and Fall became the first cabinet member sent to prison for crimes in office, over the Teapot Dome oil leases. Harding himself was never charged.
451.explanation: A president who chose to surround himself with self-serving cronies saw his administration become a byword for corruption, and his own reputation has never recovered.
451.tie_back: The kural says smallness gathers the mean-minded round itself as kin, and Harding's comfortable circle of friends is a textbook case of the company a leader chooses defining his rule.
451._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of a leader embracing unworthy associates, though the sources describe Harding as a poor judge of character rather than as base-minded himself.

452.event: At Swarthmore College, psychologist Solomon Asch asked students to say which of three lines matched a reference line, a task with an obvious answer. Unknown to each real participant, the others in the room were working with Asch and on certain trials all gave the same wrong answer. A large share of participants, about three-quarters, went along with the group's clearly false answer at least once.
452.explanation: The experiments became a classic demonstration that even a plain judgement of the senses bends toward the view of the surrounding group.
452.tie_back: As water takes on the nature of the soil it runs through, Asch's students showed their judgement taking on the colour of the company around them.
452._accuracy_note: Close to a laboratory dramatisation of the kural's claim that understanding takes the character of one's company, though it shows short-term pressure rather than lasting formation of the mind.

453.event_title: Mary, Queen of Scots, marries the Earl of Bothwell
453.event: In February 1567 Lord Darnley, husband of Mary, Queen of Scots, was killed when the house where he was staying was blown up, and James Hepburn, Earl of Bothwell, was widely held to be the chief suspect. Bothwell was acquitted at a trial with no prosecution case, and in May 1567 Mary married him. The Scottish nobles turned against the couple, Mary surrendered to them at Carberry Hill in June, was held at Lochleven Castle and was forced to abdicate in favour of her infant son in July 1567.
453.explanation: Whatever Mary herself knew, a question historians still debate, her marriage to the suspected man was enough for her subjects to judge her by him.
453.tie_back: The kural says that others cannot see into the mind and so name a person by the company they keep, and Mary lost her crown largely on the strength of whom she joined herself to.
453._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of reputation being decided by association, since her guilt has never been proven but her company condemned her in public eyes.

454.event_title: Young physicists gather at Niels Bohr's institute in Copenhagen
454.event: Niels Bohr's Institute for Theoretical Physics opened at the University of Copenhagen in 1921, and Bohr set out to make it a place where a constantly renewed group of young physicists could work together. Through the 1920s visitors from many countries, including Werner Heisenberg, Wolfgang Pauli and Paul Dirac, spent time there arguing over the problems of the atom. Much of the work that produced the new quantum mechanics in the mid-1920s was done by people who studied or debated in this circle, which they nicknamed Bohr's kindergarten.
454.explanation: One of the greatest advances in modern science grew out of a community of debate rather than from a single solitary mind.
454.tie_back: The kural says wisdom only seems to live in one's own mind but really resides in one's company, and quantum mechanics was in large part the product of the Copenhagen circle.
454._accuracy_note: A strong example of understanding sustained by a circle, though individual brilliance clearly mattered too.

455.event_title: The Clapham Sect campaigns against the slave trade
455.event: A group of evangelical Christians living near one another in Clapham, south London, including William Wilberforce, the banker Henry Thornton, James Stephen and Zachary Macaulay, centred their lives on shared worship and public causes. Many of them sat in Parliament, where they campaigned for decades against the slave trade and for reforms such as prison reform, while funding schools and missionary and Bible societies. They played a large part in the abolition of the British slave trade in 1807 and of slavery in the British Empire in 1833.
455.explanation: The members sustained one another through long years of defeat, showing how a close circle of committed people can keep both conviction and action on course.
455.tie_back: The kural says purity of mind and purity of deeds are both supported by the purity of one's company, and the Clapham neighbours kept each other's purpose and conduct steady.
455._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of a like-minded circle supporting conduct, though the sources note they were also socially conservative and part of a broader abolition movement.

456.event_title: The White Rose student resistance in Munich
456.event: In 1942 a small circle of friends at the University of Munich, including Hans and Sophie Scholl, Alexander Schmorell, Christoph Probst, Willi Graf and their professor Kurt Huber, wrote and secretly distributed leaflets urging Germans to oppose the Nazi regime. On 18 February 1943 Hans and Sophie Scholl were caught distributing the sixth leaflet at the university. They and other members were tried by the People's Court and put to death in 1943, and they are now honoured in Germany as examples of moral courage.
456.explanation: A group of friends held one another to a standard of conscience at a time when most people stayed silent, and they left a lasting example.
456.tie_back: The kural says the pure-minded leave a good legacy and those whose company is pure do no deed that is not good, and the White Rose circle acted together and is remembered together.
456._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for good company producing good deeds and a good legacy, though the group's courage cannot be credited to company alone.

457.event: Frustrated by the official Salon, a group of about thirty artists formed a cooperative society and opened their own exhibition in the former studio of the photographer Nadar on the boulevard des Capucines. Among them were Claude Monet, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Edgar Degas, Camille Pissarro, Paul Cezanne and Berthe Morisot. The show drew few visitors and hostile reviews, and a critic mocked the group as impressionists after Monet's painting Impression, Sunrise, but the name stuck and the group went on to hold eight exhibitions by 1886.
457.explanation: Artists who would have struggled alone gained a shared identity, a platform and eventually world fame by showing together.
457.tie_back: The kural says goodness of company brings every kind of renown, and the Impressionists' fame came to them as a group, under a single name.
457._accuracy_note: A reasonable illustration of renown flowing through one's circle, though it shows artistic rather than moral goodness of company.

458.event_title: Marcel Grossmann helps Einstein with the mathematics of general relativity
458.event: As students at the Zurich Polytechnic, Albert Einstein often missed lectures and relied on the careful notes of his friend Marcel Grossmann to prepare for exams. In 1912, when Einstein returned to Zurich with the physical ideas for a new theory of gravity but not the mathematics to express it, he turned to Grossmann, by then a professor of geometry, who guided him through the relevant mathematical literature. In 1913 they published a joint paper outlining the theory, with Einstein writing the physics and Grossmann the mathematical part.
458.explanation: Even one of the most original minds in history needed a trusted friend at crucial moments to make progress.
458.tie_back: The kural says that even for the wise, who already have goodness of mind, good company is a source of security and strength, and Grossmann was that support for Einstein.
458._accuracy_note: A strong illustration that even the gifted are strengthened by good company, though it concerns intellectual rather than moral support.

459.event_title: Geert Groote and the Brethren of the Common Life
459.event: After a religious conversion in 1374, the Dutch preacher Geert Groote gave up his worldly goods and began the movement later called the Devotio Moderna, which stressed meditation and the inner life. With his friend Florentius Radewyns he gathered followers who lived together, copied manuscripts for their living and prayed in common, forming the Brethren of the Common Life. The community shaped later figures such as Thomas a Kempis, the probable author of The Imitation of Christ.
459.explanation: The movement was built on the idea that a devout life is best sustained by living and working alongside others who share it.
459.tie_back: The kural says that even blessedness in the world to come, earned by goodness of mind, is made secure by good company, which is the very principle on which the Brethren lived.
459._accuracy_note: A reasonable but partial fit, since the event shows a community organised for spiritual security rather than any documented result in the next world.

460.event: In 1881 Narendranath Datta, a college student troubled by religious doubt, went to meet the teacher Sri Ramakrishna at the Kali temple in Dakshineswar. He became a frequent visitor and disciple, and Ramakrishna chose him as leader of his young followers. After Ramakrishna's death in 1886 Narendranath led them into a monastic brotherhood and, as Swami Vivekananda, went on to found the Ramakrishna Mission in 1897.
460.explanation: One meeting and the friendship that followed turned a doubting student into one of modern India's most influential spiritual leaders.
460.tie_back: The kural says there is no greater help than good company, and the company of Ramakrishna shaped the whole course of Vivekananda's life.
460._accuracy_note: A reasonable illustration of the help of good company, but it shows only the first half of the kural and not the harm of bad company.
